newsitem.title: USA: BU sees early savings in LILCO merger.
newsitem.headline: BU sees early savings in LILCO merger.

text.p: The head of Brooklyn Union Gas told a hearing Friday its proposed merger with Long Island Lighting Co (LILCO) would produce early savings through cheaper gas purchasing costs and job reductions.
Robert Catell, Brooklyn Union's chief executive officer, estimated cheaper gas prices, discounted for the combined company, would result in about one third of the initial savings seen after a merger.
Another third of the savings would come from job reductions, and the rest from other operating and administrative efficiences.
Catell was speaking in Brooklyn at a hearing arranged by the New York State Assembly Energy Committee.
He reiterated that long-term savings from the merger would add up to about $1 billion over 10 years.
Catell estimated about 600 employees from both companies, most of them in middle management, would be let go through early retirement and voluntary severance packages.
"It will be more tilted toward Long Island," said Catell, referring to where most of the job cuts are likely to occur.
"We are trying not to eliminate people from the field."
On December 29, 1996, Brooklyn Union and LILCO agreed to merge in a stock deal that would create a gas and electric company with 2.2 million customers and about $4.5 billion in annual revenue.

The merger still requires approval of the Long Island Power Authority (LIPA), New York State Public Service Commission (NYPSC), the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) and the Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC).
Brooklyn Union and LILCO said earlier they hoped to have regulatory approval for the merger within 12 to 18 months.
Separately, Catell said any refund to LILCO from a local lawsuit against Suffolk County on Long Island and Brookhaven Township would be passed on as savings to Long Island customers.
Last November a state judge ordered Suffolk County and Brookhaven to refund LILCO up to $1.1 billion in property taxes for its Shorham nuclear power plant, which was built but never opened.
